items.title: Joseph Wang, Kitchener
notes:
J. Wang appeared before the Committee and provided a presentation on Automated Speed Enforcement (ASE). He expressed concerns with obstructed signage, a flawed and misleading appeals process, and the perception that enforcement is revenue-focused rather than safety-focused. He recommended improvements including clearer signage, greater use of police enforcement, and a fairer appeal system with in-person or phone options.

In response to a Committee question, Doug Spooner, Acting Commissioner of Transportation Services, clarified that while the ASE process begins through an online portal, there is also an opportunity to speak directly with a person, and it is not limited to online appeals.

items.title: Robert Shantz, Wilmot
notes: R. Shantz appeared before the Committee regarding a speeding ticket he received through a municipal speed camera in Wilmot. He expressed concern about the use of technology such as facial recognition in enforcement in some parts of the United States and urged caution to ensure it does not advance in that direction. He noted his $88.25 ticket, described his experience with the screening and appeal process, and emphasized his concern that the program not be expanded further.

items.title: PDL-GDS-25-010, Funding for Woolwich owned Linear Wastewater Infrastructure in Breslau
notes:
Rod Regier, Commissioner of Planning, Development and Legislative Services, spoke to the report and highlighted long-term planning for growth on the east side of the Grand River. He noted the Township’s completion of an environmental assessment for extending the sanitary trunk along Fountain Street to Meadow Street, serving the airport, nearby industrial areas, and residential growth. He explained that while airport lands are federally regulated and exempt from development charges, the Region has historically partnered with the Township on oversizing and local infrastructure. He added that the proposed work would eliminate the need for a new pumping station, previously budgeted at $15 million, resulting in significant capital savings.

Members of the Committee deliberated on the report. In response to questions, R. Regier noted that the projects have been included in the long-term capital budget for the airport. He stated that reserves can accommodate the cost, and that planned future expenditures are being re-evaluated, with a full briefing to be provided to Council through the budget process.

In response to a Committee question regarding Township agreement to point three of the recommendation, R. Regier noted that initial discussions with the Township contemplated sharing half of the project’s capital costs, estimated at $50 million. He advised that while local development charges for airside development at the airport may total approximately $8 million, further discussions with the Township will be required to determine funding mechanisms and collaboration, and external support will likely be necessary. Mathieu Goetzke, Acting Chief Administrative Officer, added that he has met with the Township CAO regarding this mechanism and confirmed it responds to the Township’s needs for this phase

Responding to questions regarding how cost sharing would work if airport development were not exempt from federal development charges, R. Regier advised that new development at the airport would be treated as private development and subject to local development charges.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Equitable Services and Opportunities
COR-CFN-25-011, Development Charge Rate and Reserve Fund Sustainability Report
notes:
W. Steffler, Commissioner, Corporate Services and Chief Financial Officer, introduced the report and highlighted financial pressures on funding growth-related infrastructure. He noted that the current DC by-law, adopted in 2019 and expiring in 2029, has only been adjusted by index while costs for major projects such as transit, airport, and police have increased significantly. With a $172 million reserve against $1.6 billion in commitments and 26% of annual DC collections already consumed by debt servicing, cash flow challenges are expected to grow, including a projected $21 million impact from delayed residential collections. He emphasized the need to update the DC by-law to reflect current costs, address emerging needs, and maintain financial capacity to deliver infrastructure in step with growth.

In response to questions from the Committee, W. Steffler noted that he was not aware of any provincial work related to four-unit projects but would look into it. He confirmed that staff are preparing a long-term fiscal plan, to be highlighted in the 2026 capital budget process, with further discussion to come. He also explained the role of DC reserves and the challenges created when collections are received at the end of a project.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Resilient and Future Ready Organization
COR-TRY-25-022, Debenture Financing up to 30 years
notes:
W. Steffler spoke to the report, outlining proposed changes to the debt policy. He highlighted that the current 10 to 20 year terms would be expanded to allow up to 30 years for large infrastructure projects with long useful lives, and that this approach would better align repayment with asset lifespans, smooth annual debt costs, and reduce taxpayer impacts. He noted that longer terms would be used selectively and in compliance with regulations, while shorter terms would remain for other financing needs. It was further noted that the change would provide flexibility in future financial planning while maintaining the Region’s financial stability and AAA credit rating.

In response to a question from the Committee regarding how projects would be selected for 30-year terms and whether staff would receive delegated authority, W. Steffler explained that projects must meet established criteria and regulatory requirements for issuing debentures, as is currently the case with 10- and 20-year terms. He noted that eligibility would be identified through the debenture process, with the 30-year option added where appropriate. He further stated that creditors require assurance that proper assets back the debt, and a legal review process is in place to ensure alignment.

items.title: Councillor C. James Motion
notes:
C. James introduced her Notice of Motion on respect in healthy democracy. She highlighted the increasing harassment and threats faced by elected officials, noting impacts on safety, public trust, and willingness to serve. She emphasized that while debate is part of democracy, respect must remain central, and called on Council to reaffirm a culture of integrity, reject abuse and hate, and ensure all people feel safe and welcome to serve. She further added that her motion be forwarded to all area municipalities.

Members of the Committee deliberated in support.

items.title: Councillor C. James Notice of Motion
notes:
C. James introduced her Notice of Motion regarding the Automated Speed Enforcement (ASE) program. She noted confusion among the public about signage and program rules, and emphasized the need for greater transparency and consistency across municipalities. She highlighted that while the Province has passed legislation, further standardization is needed to reduce confusion and improve effectiveness. C. James described the motion as an advocacy piece to the Province, requesting standardization of the ASE program in partnership with municipalities.

P. Wolf stated she was opposed to the motion and explained her reasons.

motions.text: WHEREAS democracy is healthy when everyone is able to participate fully and safely and contribute to the well-being of their community; AND WHEREAS we are witnessing the dissolution of democratic discourse and respectful debate across all levels of government and in neighbouring jurisdictions; AND WHEREAS Ontario’s municipally elected officials are dealing with increasingly hostile, unsafe environments facing threats, violence and harassment; AND WHEREAS social media platforms have exacerbated disrespectful dialogue, negative commentary, and toxic engagement which disincentivizes individuals, especially women and candidates from varying backgrounds from running for office; AND WHEREAS better decisions are made when democracy is respectful and constructive and the voices of diverse genders, identities, ethnicities, races, ages and abilities are heard and represented around municipal council tables; AND WHEREAS there are reports and data indicating an increase in harassment and intimidation incidents targeting politicians; AND WHEREAS the Association of Municipalities of Ontario’s Healthy Democracy Project has identified concerning trends with fewer people voting in local elections and running for municipal office; NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: THAT the Regional Municipality of Waterloo council affirms that a healthy democracy requires the full, safe, and respectful participation of all individuals, and that hostility, harassment, and violence directed toward elected officials, candidates, and community members are direct threats to democratic integrity; AND THAT the Region of Waterloo Council formally endorses and adopts the Elect Respect pledge and commits to advancing a culture of civic engagement rooted in respect, and accountability by: • Modeling respect and integrity in all interactions, public, private, and online; • Actively rejecting and denouncing all forms of abuse, harassment, hate, intimidation, and violence; • Upholding constructive discourse by debating ideas and policies rather than engaging in personal attacks; • Creating inclusive and supportive conditions that encourage and protect the participation of individuals from all genders, identities, races, ethnicities, ages, abilities, and backgrounds in local democracy; • Advocating for robust protections and appropriate responses from law enforcement and governing bodies when threats or harassment occur against elected officials or candidates; and • Holding ourselves and each other accountable to the highest standards of ethical leadership and respectful governance. AND THAT the Region of Waterloo Council calls upon all elected officials, community organizations, and institutions, to endorse and promote the Elect Respect campaign; AND THAT this resolution be forwarded to the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, Ontario’s Big City Mayors, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, area MPs and MPPs, Waterloo Regional Police Service, Ontario Provincial Police, Wellington County municipalities, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to urge coordinated and sustained action in defending democratic engagement and the safety of elected officials.

motions.item_title: Councillor C. James Notice of Motion
motions.text: Whereas municipalities across Ontario are increasingly adopting Automated Speed Enforcement (ASE) programs as a proven tool to improve road safety, particularly in school zones and community safety zones; Whereas reducing vehicle speeds helps creates calmer , safer neighbhourhoods that encourage people to use active forms of transportation and to be active in their communities; Whereas the Region of Waterloo has operated an ASE program since 2021 in partnership with local area municipalities, working closely with the Ontario Traffic Council to adopt and promote best practices; Whereas the Region of Waterloo’s Strategic Plan “Growing with Care” highlights Climate Aligned Growth, calling for the development of complete streets and expanded alternative transportation networks that reduce reliance on cars. The Plan also emphasizes Equitable Services and Opportunities by prioritizing inclusive, accessible services that support community health, safety, and complete communities. The ASE program directly supports these goals by calming traffic, protecting vulnerable road users, and enabling active transportation; Whereas the current legislative and regulatory framework, enabled by the Highway Traffic Act, allows municipalities to operate ASE programs and to independently determine key elements of program delivery; Whereas the Region continues to hear from the community both the need for stronger traffic calming in neighbourhoods and the need for transparency and clarity around ASE program operations; Whereas some municipalities across Ontario have implemented ASE programs with varying approaches, which presents an opportunity to promote consistency and alignment with emerging best practices province-wide; Whereas a program review of ASE operations could increase transparency, public understanding, and trust, and better support the program’s intended outcomes of road safety and speed reduction; Whereas the Government of Ontario passed Bill 34 (Transportation for the Future Act, 2024) on June 5, 2025, introducing new provisions under the Highway Traffic Act (Part XIV.5 – Automated Camera Enforcement for Road Safety), which emphasize transparency and enable new ministerial powers regarding ASE and Red Light Camera programs, with regulations expected in Fall 2025; Therefore be it resolved that the Regional Municipality of Waterloo respectfully request the Province of Ontario, through the Ministry of Transportation to continue to work collaboratively with municipalities that operate ASE programs to: Review and enhance existing regulated signage requirements to improve clarity and understanding for motorists; Establish public reporting requirements that would both enhance public understanding and increase program integrity; Engage with municipalities, road safety experts, law enforcement and adjudication professionals to review the program, including the Highway Traffic Act and relevant regulations to ensure the standards reflect local safety needs while providing province-wide consistency; Provide guidance and tools to support municipalities in standardizing operations with best practices and in enhancing public education around ASE operations; Introduce regulatory requirements to ensure that revenues generated from ASE programs are directed toward local road safety initiatives. And that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Minister of Transportation, Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), all Ontario municipalities with ASE programs, local MPPs, and the Ontario Traffic Council.
motions.text_html:
Whereas municipalities across Ontario are increasingly adopting Automated Speed Enforcement (ASE) programs as a proven tool to improve road safety, particularly in school zones and community safety zones;
Whereas reducing vehicle speeds helps creates calmer , safer neighbhourhoods that encourage people to use active forms of transportation and to be active in their communities;
Whereas the Region of Waterloo has operated an ASE program since 2021 in partnership with local area municipalities, working closely with the Ontario Traffic Council to adopt and promote best practices;
Whereas the Region of Waterloo’s Strategic Plan “Growing with Care” highlights Climate Aligned Growth, calling for the development of complete streets and expanded alternative transportation networks that reduce reliance on cars. The Plan also emphasizes Equitable Services and Opportunities by prioritizing inclusive, accessible services that support community health, safety, and complete communities. The ASE program directly supports these goals by calming traffic, protecting vulnerable road users, and enabling active transportation;
Whereas the current legislative and regulatory framework, enabled by the Highway Traffic Act, allows municipalities to operate ASE programs and to independently determine key elements of program delivery;
Whereas the Region continues to hear from the community both the need for stronger traffic calming in neighbourhoods and the need for transparency and clarity around ASE program operations;
Whereas some municipalities across Ontario have implemented ASE programs with varying approaches, which presents an opportunity to promote consistency and alignment with emerging best practices province-wide;
Whereas a program review of ASE operations could increase transparency, public understanding, and trust, and better support the program’s intended outcomes of road safety and speed reduction;
Whereas the Government of Ontario passed Bill 34 (Transportation for the Future Act, 2024) on June 5, 2025, introducing new provisions under the Highway Traffic Act (Part XIV.5 – Automated Camera Enforcement for Road Safety), which emphasize transparency and enable new ministerial powers regarding ASE and Red Light Camera programs, with regulations expected in Fall 2025;
Therefore be it resolved that the Regional Municipality of Waterloo respectfully request the Province of Ontario, through the Ministry of Transportation to continue to work collaboratively with municipalities that operate ASE programs to:

  1. Review and enhance existing regulated signage requirements to improve clarity and understanding for motorists;
  2. Establish public reporting requirements that would both enhance public understanding and increase program integrity;
  3. Engage with municipalities, road safety experts, law enforcement and adjudication professionals to review the program, including the Highway Traffic Act and relevant regulations to ensure the standards reflect local safety needs while providing province-wide consistency;
  4. Provide guidance and tools to support municipalities in standardizing operations with best practices and in enhancing public education around ASE operations;
  5. Introduce regulatory requirements to ensure that revenues generated from ASE programs are directed toward local road safety initiatives.
    And that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Minister of Transportation, Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), all Ontario municipalities with ASE programs, local MPPs, and the Ontario Traffic Council.
